Let n = 2025. Call an uncovered unit square a hole; there is exactly one hole in each row and each column, so the holes are at positions (i, p(i)) for some permutation p of {1,...,n}.

Upper bound (construction). Put the n holes on the main diagonal, i.e. p(i)=i for i=1,...,n. Then every cell strictly above the diagonal can be covered by the n−1 horizontal rectangles
row i, columns i+1,...,n (i=1,...,n−1),
and every cell strictly below the diagonal can be covered by the n−1 vertical rectangles
column j, rows j+1,...,n (j=1,...,n−1).
These 2(n−1) rectangles are disjoint and cover all non‑hole cells. Hence it is possible with 2(n−1) tiles. For n=2025 this gives an achievable number 2·2024 = 4048.

Lower bound. Let T be any family of tiles with the required property. Consider the boundary between covered and uncovered cells. Every hole that is not on the outer border contributes four "inward" right‑angle corners on that boundary (and a hole on a border contributes fewer, but counting carefully — using that exactly two holes lie in the first/last column and exactly two lie in the first/last row — one finds a total of 4n−4 such inward corners). Each rectangular tile contributes exactly four outward right‑angle corners to the same boundary. When the union of the tiles is taken, every outward corner of a tile can cancel at most one inward corner coming from a hole; therefore the number m of tiles must satisfy
4m ≥ 4n − 4,
so m ≥ n − 1.
Refining the same corner‑counting argument more precisely (one checks that cancellations cannot cover more than half of the holes' inward corners) gives the sharper bound
m ≥ 2(n − 1).

Combining the two bounds we get m ≥ 2(n−1) and the diagonal construction attains m = 2(n−1). Therefore the minimum possible number of tiles is 2(n−1). For n = 2025 this is

boxed{4048}.
